note: Lectures, links, objectives, concepts and case studies are extracted from the notes; themes, takeaways and the system boxes come from game/content/knowledge.yml. Do not edit by hand.

lectures.title: The AI-engineering landscape and the course toolchain
takeaways: A model is a small part of a system whose bulk is data infrastructure, evaluation and operations, and that is where the effort and the failures concentrate.
Engineering data drifts, needs calibration and carries physical units, which widens the gap between a validated model and a working system.
lectures.data: UCI Air Quality, a gas sensor array on an Italian roadside
objectives: Map the end-to-end lifecycle of an engineering ML system and identify the standardized toolchain used throughout the semester.
Contrast "a model in a notebook" with "a system," naming the data contracts, drift, and monitoring concerns that separate them.
Explain why engineering data imposes provenance and traceability requirements that general-purpose ML tutorials ignore.
Justify each component of the course toolchain in terms of the failure it prevents.

lectures.title: Reproducible environments and version control
takeaways: Reproducible means you can say which data, code and settings produced a number, and produce it again.
Lock the environment with uv, keep code, data and models in tools that suit each, and log every run.
lectures.data: The Air Quality data from Lecture 1
objectives: Build and lock a project environment with `uv`, and rebuild it exactly on a fresh machine.
Choose the right versioning tool for code, data, and models, and explain why large binary files do not belong in plain git.
Turn an exploratory notebook into a script or package with a tested command-line entry point.
Log a run to MLflow so that one run equals the same exact fact you can always reproduce.

lectures.title: Databases for engineering data
takeaways: A relational database is a contract you can query; store readings in long form, keyed by sensor and time.
Types with physical meaning prevent a class of bugs, but a type is not a validation.
lectures.data: Intel Berkeley Lab sensor readings, in PostgreSQL
objectives: Model sensor/simulation data in a relational schema with appropriate types (timestamps, numeric precision, units).
Load data into PostgreSQL and query it with SQL: joins, `GROUP BY`, window functions, time bucketing.
Reason about indexing and query cost for time-range queries.

lectures.title: Database landscape
takeaways: Match the storage layout to the access pattern; a row store suits live writes, a column store suits scans over history.
Parquet with DuckDB reads only the columns and row groups a query needs.
lectures.data: Intel Berkeley Lab readings, in Parquet and DuckDB
objectives: Explain the row-store versus column-store trade-off and why a columnar layout is faster to scan, and read and write Parquet.
Query Parquet with DuckDB, and choose between a transactional (OLTP) and an analytical (OLAP) tool.
Name the other kinds of store (document, key-value, time-series) and say when each one fits.

lectures.title: Dataframes and batch pipelines
takeaways: Describe the work and let a planner decide how to run it; vectorized and lazy code gets the speed back.
Small, pure, idempotent stages make a pipeline safe to rerun after a failure.
lectures.data: The Tennessee Eastman plant, with Polars
objectives: Get more familiar with pandas and, most importantly, write Polars code that operates on whole columns at once instead of row by row, including grouping and joining.
Break a data pipeline into small steps that each read one file and write one file, so a run that fails halfway through can be started again without corrupting anything.
Explain the difference between pandas running code immediately and Polars planning a computation before running it, and use that difference to choose between the two for a given task.

lectures.title: Streaming data and data validation
takeaways: Streaming handles data that is never finished; windows in event time, closed by watermarks, cope with late and out-of-order readings.
Validation is an executable gate that fails loudly before bad data reaches a model.
lectures.data: The Intel Lab feed, most of it out of order
objectives: Distinguish batch from streaming, and identify when sensor systems require streaming.
Explain windowing, event vs. processing time, watermarks, and late or out-of-order data.
Author executable data-quality checks and integrate them as a pipeline gate.

lectures.title: Features for time-series models
takeaways: A dynamic process needs its own past in the table, as lagged columns.
Ask of every column whether it could have been known at the row's timestamp; if not, it is leakage.
objectives: Explain why a dynamic process needs its own past in the feature table, and a steady-state measurement does not.
Build a feature table from a sensor log in which every value in a row was knowable at that row's timestamp, dropping the rows whose past lies outside the record.
Convert the two coefficients of a fitted first-order model into a time constant and a gain, and say whether they are physically plausible.

lectures.title: The machine learning (ML) workflow I: Time series
takeaways: A forecast is supervised learning with a horizon, and it earns its place only by beating persistence and the mean.
Score forecasts on time-ordered splits; a shuffled split leaks the future.
lectures.data: Reactor pressure from the Tennessee Eastman plant
objectives: Frame a time-series forecast as a supervised learning problem, stating the horizon and what is known when the forecast is made.
Compare a forecasting model against persistence and mean baselines across horizons, and say whether the model earned its place.
Choose between direct and recursive multi-step forecasting, and explain why recursive errors grow with the horizon.
Evaluate a forecaster with a time-ordered split whose gap is at least the horizon, and explain why a shuffled split inflates the score.
Use forecast residuals as a simple anomaly detector, setting the threshold on normal data and reporting false alarms and detection delay.

lectures.title: The machine learning (ML) workflow II: Regression
takeaways: Every scikit-learn model is fitted and scored the same way, so the split, the features and the metric decide the result.
Hold out whole groups when the model will meet new groups; a random split can reverse which model wins.
lectures.data: The concrete strength dataset and Tennessee Eastman reactor pressure
objectives: Frame an engineering question as regression or classification, and name its samples, features and target.
Split data into training, validation and test sets, and explain why the test set is used only once.
Fit and compare linear, decision tree, neural network and Gaussian process models through scikit-learn's common `fit` and `predict` interface, on a table of experiments and on a NARX table.
Write the training of a linear model, a neural network and a Gaussian process as an optimization problem, and say what each one optimizes.
Use k-fold and grouped cross-validation, validation curves and learning curves to diagnose underfitting and overfitting and to choose between models.

lectures.title: The machine learning (ML) workflow III: Classification, experiment tracking and hyperparameter search/tuning
takeaways: Accuracy hides the kind of mistake; the confusion matrix, precision, recall and the threshold show it.
Search hyperparameters with Optuna, record every trial in MLflow, and test the winner once.
lectures.data: Faults in the Tennessee Eastman plant
objectives: Explain what a classifier predicts (a class, from a probability and a threshold), and read a logistic regression's decision boundary on one plant signal.
Say what each of the four model families minimizes when it classifies.
Understand a confusion matrix, and the concepts of accuracy, precision and recall from it.
Move the decision threshold to trade missed faults against false alarms.
Explain why a classifier can miss faults it was never trained on.
Run a hyperparameter search with Optuna, record every trial in MLflow, and register the best model.

lectures.title: ML with PyTorch/JAX
takeaways: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation gives every gradient exactly for about the cost of two forward passes.
PyTorch and JAX implement the same mathematics with different designs, and a training loop breaks in a few known ways.
objectives: Explain what a backward pass computes by applying the chain rule to a small network, and why reverse mode suits a scalar loss better than finite differences.

Contrast how PyTorch (a recorded tape that accumulates into `.grad`) and JAX (transformations of pure functions) compute the same gradient, and use that to explain `zero_grad()`, `no_grad()` and immutable arrays.
Work with tensor shapes, broadcasting, dtypes and devices, and read a shape error.
Write a training loop in PyTorch and in JAX, and say what each of Adam's hyperparameters does.
Diagnose a training failure that raises no error by comparing against an exact reference, the predict-the-mean baseline, or a grouped split.
Measure whether an accelerator helps before moving a model onto one.

lectures.title: ML architectures for engineering data
takeaways: Match the architecture to the structure of the input, an MLP for a vector, a CNN for a field, a 1D-CNN or RNN for a sequence.
Train with a schedule, early stopping and clipping, and check the architecture beats a simple baseline.
lectures.data: Turbofan engines and their remaining useful life
objectives: Match model architecture to the structure of the input (vector, field/image, sequence).
Implement a 1D-CNN or RNN for sensor time series and a 2D-CNN for field/image data.
Apply regularization and normalization appropriate to each architecture.

lectures.title: Scientific machine learning: PINNs, neural ODEs and neural DAEs
takeaways: Scientific machine learning keeps the mechanistic model and learns only the unknown term.
A PINN favors the physics through its loss but does not enforce it; constraints can be built into the network instead.
objectives: Explain what a physics-informed neural network (PINN) minimizes, and why its physics holds only approximately.
Build a PINN in JAX and compare its extrapolation with a plain network.
Derive a neural ODE from a recurrent network by letting the time step go to zero, and train one with a differentiable ODE solver.
Explain why some physics must be enforced rather than penalized, and what makes a model a differential-algebraic equation (DAE).
Contrast the sequential and simultaneous approaches to training a dynamic model.
Train a neural DAE with SiNDAE, and check that its predictions satisfy the constraints.
Compare PINNs, neural ODEs, neural DAEs and projection layers: where the physics lives, and what each one guarantees.

lectures.title: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for machine learning
takeaways: An uncertainty is a claim about coverage, and calibration on held-out data is the only test of it.
Gaussian processes, ensembles and conformal prediction each make a different assumption about the region they cannot see.
objectives: Define uncertainty quantification, distinguish aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty, and tell confidence, credible and prediction intervals apart.
Check whether a predictive uncertainty is calibrated, with coverage, a reliability diagram and a proper scoring rule, and recalibrate it with one scale factor.
Explain what a Gaussian process's band promises, and recognize three ways it fails: heteroscedastic noise, a misspecified kernel, and too few data.
Explain what the spread of a bootstrap or a deep ensemble measures, and why it needs a noise term and recalibration before it is an interval.
Wrap any model in split conformal or CV+ prediction intervals, and state the exchangeability condition their guarantee rests on.
Fit and compare UQ-capable regressors from pycse on data inside and beyond the training range.

lectures.title: Bayesian optimization
takeaways: Bayesian optimization is for expensive, noisy objectives without gradients, when the budget is tens of evaluations.
A Gaussian process and an acquisition function choose the next experiment, balancing exploration against exploitation.
objectives: Explain what Bayesian optimization (BO) is, why it is called Bayesian, and when it beats gradient-based and other derivative-free optimizers: expensive, noisy, black-box objectives with a budget of tens of evaluations.
Explain the BO loop (a Gaussian-process surrogate, an acquisition function, evaluate, update) and the trade-off between exploration and exploitation.

Write and compute the common acquisition functions: probability of improvement (PI), expected improvement (EI) and upper and lower confidence bounds (UCB, LCB), and explain how their parameters set the balance between exploration and exploitation.
Run BO in BoTorch on an engineering problem and compare it with random search over several seeds.
Name the extensions engineers need (constraints, batches, several objectives, several fidelities) and recognize where BO is used across engineering and science.

lectures.title: Generative AI
takeaways: A generative model learns the distribution of the data, and conditioning it answers questions in any direction.
Gaussian mixtures condition exactly on any variables; flow matching scales further but answers only the question it was trained for.
lectures.data: The roots of the Peng-Robinson equation and a batch reactor
objectives: Distinguish a generative model from the regression and classification models of L8–L14, and explain why a regression model gives a wrong answer to an inverse question with more than one solution.
Fit a Gaussian mixture model to the joint distribution of inputs and outputs, choose the number of components, and condition it to sample the inputs that give a target output.
Explain how flow matching turns samples of a simple distribution into samples of the data, train one with a mean-squared-error loss, and sample it by integrating an ODE.
Pose root finding, optimization and parameter estimation as conditional sampling, and check the samples against the physical model.
Place generative models in the machine-learning landscape, and explain why they are as dependent on data, and as limited by it, as any regression model.
Describe how generative models are used for images, molecules, proteins, materials and weather, and the failure modes those uses share.

lectures.title: Large language models (LLMs): what they are and how they are trained
takeaways: An LLM is a generative model of text that predicts the next token, one token at a time.
Fluent is not the same as true; hallucination follows from next-token prediction.
lectures.data: A tiny GPT, trained from scratch on the notes of Lectures 1 to 16
objectives: Describe an LLM as a generative model of text: the chain rule turns the probability of a text into a product of next-token probabilities, and generation samples from them one token at a time.
Explain what tokens are, how byte-pair encoding builds them, and why the context window is a budget counted in tokens.
Explain pretraining: next-token cross-entropy at every position of every context window, on the transformer of L12 with a causal mask.
Relate model size, training data and compute across language models, and explain what post-training adds to a pretrained model.
Explain what temperature does to the next-token distribution, and why hallucination follows from next-token prediction.

lectures.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): answering from your documents
takeaways: An LLM answers from its context window, so the answer is bounded by the passages put there.
Keyword and embedding search fail differently; fusing them and re-ranking, measured on a gold set, beats either.
objectives: Explain context engineering: an LLM answers from what is in its context window, so deciding what goes there, and how it gets there, determines the answer.
Give a model a tool, explain the tool-call exchange, and recognize when fetching context on demand (reading files, searching the web) is the right design, and the prompt-injection risk it brings.

Build keyword search (an inverted index with BM25) and semantic search (embeddings), combine them, and rerank the result with a cross-encoder; explain where late interaction (ColBERT) sits between them.
Choose chunk size, embedding model and index from measured trade-offs in hit rate, memory and search time, and say what changes when the index moves to a server.
Assemble a grounded prompt with citations within a token budget, and measure retrieval with hit@k and MRR on a gold set of queries.
Trace each stage of a retrieval pipeline running in the browser: what runs at build time, what runs on the page, and what each costs.

lectures.title: LLM agents: tools, loops, harnesses and coding agents
takeaways: An agent is an LLM that calls tools in a loop and chooses each next step from the last result.
The harness around the model, its permissions, caching and checks, is most of the system.
lectures.data: Choosing the tilt of solar panels on a roof
objectives: Explain what an LLM agent is, and when a fixed workflow is the better choice.
Trace the agent loop, and name the jobs of the harness, the software around the model.
Explain how prompt caching cuts the cost of a long agent run, and what breaks the cache.
Write tool definitions a model can use correctly, and guard an agent that can act: least privilege, a person's approval, and no lethal trifecta.
Describe the parts of a coding agent: the instructions file, the tools, the permissions and sandbox, and context management.
Set up a project so a coding agent can work in it safely, with the course's toolchain: uv, git, tests and read-only data.

themes.name: The system around the model
themes.blurb: The model is a small part of a production system; the data, checks and operations around it are most of the work and most of the failures.

themes.name: Reproducibility and tracking
themes.blurb: Rebuild the exact environment, version code, data and models separately, and record every run so a number can be traced and produced again.

themes.name: Storing engineering data
themes.blurb: Pick the store that matches the access pattern, a row store for live writes and lookups, a column store and Parquet for scans over history.

themes.name: Pipelines and streams
themes.blurb: Turn raw logs into answers with stages that are fast, safe to rerun, and correct when data arrives late and out of order.

themes.name: Data validation and leakage
themes.blurb: Check data before it reaches a model, and make sure no column could not have been known at the time it claims.

themes.name: Dynamic processes and features
themes.blurb: A process with memory needs its own past in the table, built as lags that respect time, runs and the question being asked.

themes.name: Forecasting
themes.blurb: A forecast is supervised learning with a horizon; it earns its place only by beating persistence and the mean, scored on time-ordered splits.

themes.name: The machine learning workflow
themes.blurb: Fit, split, score; the split, the features and the metric decide the result more than the choice of model.

themes.name: Optimization and training
themes.blurb: Training is optimization; automatic differentiation gives exact gradients, and a training loop has a few steps that each break in a known way.

themes.name: Neural architectures
themes.blurb: Match the architecture to the structure of the input, a vector, a field or a sequence, and check that it beats a simple baseline.

themes.name: Physics and machine learning
themes.blurb: Keep the mechanistic model and learn only the unknown part, with the physics in the loss, in the solver, or enforced by the network.

themes.name: Uncertainty quantification
themes.blurb: An uncertainty is a claim about how often the truth falls in an interval, and only held-out data can test it.

themes.name: Optimizing experiments
themes.blurb: When each evaluation is an expensive experiment, a surrogate and an acquisition function spend a small budget where it can still learn or gain.

themes.name: Generative models
themes.blurb: Learn the distribution of the data, not one function of it, and condition it to answer questions in any direction.

themes.name: Language models
themes.blurb: An LLM predicts the next token; fluency comes from that, and so does confident text that is not true.

themes.name: Retrieval and context
themes.blurb: An answer is only as good as the passages in the context window, so fetching and ranking them is engineering you can measure.

themes.name: Agents and coding agents
themes.blurb: An agent is an LLM calling tools in a loop; the harness around it, its permissions and its checks, is most of the system.
